walkthroughs.body_html:
Space Physics — a core area of GCSE Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Space Physics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Space Physics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Redshift of distant galaxies is evidence that:
options: the universe is contracting
galaxies are heating up
the universe is expanding
light slows over distance

mcqs.q: The Sun is currently in which stage?
options: Protostar
Main sequence
Red giant
White dwarf

mcqs.q: If an object is moving at constant velocity in a straight line, what is the net force on it?
options: The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
There must be a forward force on the object to keep it moving.
Zero — by Newton's first law, constant velocity requires zero net force.
Velocity is always conserved in any collision.

mcqs.q: In a collision between two objects, what quantity is always conserved (in a closed system)?
options: The nucleus shrinks to half its original size after one half-life.
Velocity is always conserved in any collision.
Kinetic energy is always conserved in collisions because energy is conserved.
Total momentum is always conserved; kinetic energy is only conserved in elastic collisions.

mcqs.q: After one half-life, what happens to an individual radioactive nucleus?
options: The nucleus shrinks to half its original size after one half-life.
It has a 50 percent chance of having decayed — radioactive decay is random for any single nucleus.
Every nucleus is guaranteed to have half-decayed after one half-life.
Velocity is always conserved in any collision.
